lines.text: In open world games, you can smash into a wall and just keep driving. Real cars are designed to wreck themselves on purpose.
In a crash, your body must go from full speed to zero. What hurts is how fast it stops.
Stop almost instantly and the force is enormous. Stretch the stop out, even slightly, and the force drops dramatically.
That's the crumple zone: the front and back of the car are designed to fold and absorb the energy.
But the cabin is the opposite: a stiff safety cell of high strength steel that's meant to keep its shape.
Seat belts and airbags then stretch your own stop a little longer.
A Mercedes engineer patented the idea, and it first reached a production car in 1959.
